hints: Notice the reactants here, a hydroxide ion and a polar bromoalkane. What type of mechanism does this suggest?
Identify who is electron rich and who is electron poor. The $\text{OH}^-$ has lone pairs and the C attached to Br is $\text{C}^{\delta+}$.
Remember curly arrows always flow from electrons to an electron deficient site, while the $\text{C-Br}$ bond must break to put both electrons on bromine.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the reaction type**

This is nucleophilic substitution of a primary halogenoalkane. Hydroxide is the nucleophile and replaces Br to form an alcohol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$$

**Spot the nucleophile and electrophile**

$\text{OH}^-$ is electron rich with three lone pairs, so it is the electron donor. The C bonded to Br is $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ because Br is more electronegative, so it is the electron acceptor.

**Apply the curly arrow rules**

A curly arrow must start at a lone pair or a bond, never at a positive atom. So the first arrow starts at a lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ and points to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ atom. A second arrow starts at the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and points to Br to show heterolytic fission forming $\text{Br}^-$.

options.A: Correct. The nucleophile donates electrons, so the arrow goes from a lone pair on OH- to the electrophilic C delta+ atom. This shows the start of bond formation in the SN2 step.
options.B: Incorrect. Curly arrows show movement of electrons, so they cannot start at the C delta+ atom which is electron poor. This reverses the correct direction of electron flow.
options.C: Incorrect. When the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically, both electrons go to the more electronegative Br to form Br-. An arrow pointing back to C would incorrectly keep the electrons on carbon.
options.D: Incorrect. Homolytic fission gives free radicals with one electron each and needs UV light or high temperature. This reaction is polar nucleophilic substitution, so fission is heterolytic to give ions.
